sets.title: Robots in the Kitchen
text: For years, robots have taken {{1}} in car factories and warehouses, performing repetitive tasks that humans used to do. Now they are moving into a far more personal space: the kitchen. Several companies have recently managed to launch kitchen robots onto the {{2}}, machines that can chop vegetables, stir sauces and even plate up a finished meal without any human help.

The robots are not cheap; {{3}}, many experts believe prices will fall quickly as production increases. This is largely due {{4}} advances in artificial intelligence and sensor technology, which allow the machines to recognise ingredients and adjust cooking times automatically. Engineers had to figure {{5}} how to make the robotic arms move smoothly without spilling anything, and early models often splashed sauce across the worktop.

When the first versions appeared, they moved so slowly that many customers soon lost {{6}} in the idea, and some critics said the whole trend had got {{7}} of hand. Despite this, manufacturers remain confident. The device comes with a two-year {{8}}, so customers can get it repaired free of charge if anything goes wrong, and most reviewers agree that the technology is improving fast.

why: Correct: 'take part in' is a fixed phrase meaning to participate in something.
You 'play' a role, not 'take' one, so 'role' does not fit this fixed phrase.
'Take a share in' means to own part of a business; it does not fit this meaning.
'Piece' is never used in this fixed phrase.
Correct: 'launch something onto the market' is the fixed collocation for making a new product available to buy.
'Onto the trade' is not a natural collocation.
You launch a product onto the market, not onto an industry; 'onto the industry' is not correct.
'Onto the business' is not a natural collocation.
Correct: 'however' introduces the contrast between the robots being expensive now and experts' prediction that prices will fall.
'Moreover' adds a similar idea; it does not fit a contrast.
'Therefore' signals a result, but falling prices are not a logical consequence of being expensive.
'Instead' signals replacement, not contrast between two different claims.
Correct: 'due to' is a fixed phrase meaning 'because of'.
'Due with' does not exist.
'Due for' means 'expected to happen soon', a different meaning.
'Due from' is used for money or things owed, not for causes.
Correct: 'figure out' means to work out or solve a problem.
'Figure up' is not a standard phrasal verb.
'Figure in' means to be included as a factor, not to solve something.
'Figure on' means to expect or plan for something.
Correct: 'lose interest in' is the natural collocation for no longer being enthusiastic about something.
'Lose attention' is not a natural English collocation.
'Lose care' is not a standard collocation.
'Lose your mind' means to go crazy, which is not the meaning here.
Correct: 'get out of hand' is an idiom meaning to become uncontrollable.
'Get off hand' is not a real idiom.
'Get away of hand' is not correct English.
'Get over hand' is not a real idiom.
Correct: 'guarantee' is the standard word for a company's commitment to repair or replace a faulty product within a set period.
'Promise' is too general for this specific kind of consumer protection.
'Insurance' is protection you usually pay for against risk, not a manufacturer's free repair commitment.
'Assurance' means a statement that something is true, not a specific repair agreement.

sets.title: The Marathon That Changed Her Life
text: Until last year, Diane Foster had never taken part in any kind of race. She worked long hours as an accountant and rarely found time to exercise. Then a close friend persuaded her to sign {{1}} for a local 10-kilometre run, just to see what would happen.

She found the first few runs exhausting, but she refused to give {{2}} running, even when her legs ached so much that she could barely climb the stairs. Within six months, she had worked her way {{3}} to running ten kilometres without stopping, and she began to look {{4}} to her early-morning training sessions instead of dreading them.

Diane completed her first 10-kilometre race in just under an hour, and the sense of achievement {{5}} her decide to enter a half marathon a few months later. {{6}} that, she had never imagined she would one day run a full marathon, but that is exactly what happened last spring. Her story is proof {{7}} it is never too late to try something new, no matter {{8}} old you are.

why: Correct: 'sign up for something' means to register to take part in it.
'Sign down for' is not a real phrasal verb.
'Sign out' means to record your departure or log out of a system, not to register for an event.
'Sign over' means to formally transfer ownership of something to someone else.
Correct: 'give up running' means to stop/quit running; followed directly by '-ing' this way, 'up' is the only option that works.
'Give in' means to surrender to pressure and does not combine directly with a following '-ing' object like this.
'Give out' means to distribute or to stop functioning, not to quit an activity.
'Give over' is not a standard phrasal verb with this meaning.
Correct: 'work your way up to something' means to progress gradually until you reach it.
'Work your way through' usually needs an object like a book or problem, not 'to' a distance.
'Down to' means 'the responsibility of', which does not fit here.
'On to' means moving to a new topic, not gradual progress.
Correct: 'look forward to' is the fixed idiom for feeling happy about something that is going to happen, matching the contrast with 'dreading them'.
'Look ahead to' is used for longer-term planning, not personal anticipation like this.
'Look round to' is not a standard combination here.
'Look back to' means to think about the past, the opposite of anticipation.
Correct: 'make someone decide' uses the bare infinitive without 'to', which fits the sentence.
'Encouraged' would need 'encouraged her to decide', with 'to'.
'Persuaded' would need 'persuaded her to decide', with 'to'.
'Motivated' would need 'motivated her to decide', with 'to'.
Correct: 'before that' means 'up to that point', matching the time contrast with what happened later.
'Since that' is not a natural standalone time phrase (it would normally be 'since then').
'After that' would reverse the timeline, since the imagining failure happened earlier, not after.
'Until that' is grammatically incomplete on its own (it would need 'until then').
Correct: 'proof that' introduces a clause with its own subject and verb.
'Proof of' needs a noun, not a full clause like 'it is never too late'.
'Proof for' is not a natural fixed pattern.
'Proof which' cannot directly introduce a new clause like this.
Correct: 'no matter how old you are' is the fixed pattern used with an adjective like 'old'.
'No matter what' would need a noun, not an adjective describing age.
'No matter which' is used for choosing between options, not describing a quality like age.
'No matter that' is not a standard fixed phrase.

sets.title: Street Art Finds a New Audience
text: Graffiti was once seen purely as a crime, but public {{1}} has slowly begun to change. Many cities now pay professional artists to carry {{2}} projects that turn grey walls into colourful murals.

One artist, who works {{3}} the name 'Luna', has painted more than fifty murals across Europe. She says the secret of a good mural lies {{4}} choosing a location where it will catch people's attention. Local councils used to {{5}} down requests for street art almost automatically, but many now actively invite artists to submit designs.

{{6}}, not everyone agrees that graffiti belongs in galleries. Some critics argue that moving street art indoors takes {{7}} from its original purpose, which was to be free and accessible to everyone. Even so, there is no {{8}} that public interest in the art form continues to grow every year.

why: Correct: 'public perception' is what people believe or think about something, and a perception is the kind of thing that can 'change' over time.
'Attention' is paid or drawn, and usually 'shifts' rather than 'changes'.
'Awareness' usually 'grows' or 'increases', not 'changes'.
'Concern' usually 'grows' or 'eases', not 'changes'.
Correct: 'carry out a project' means to perform or execute it.
'Carry on' means to continue, and would normally need 'with' before a noun like 'projects'.
'Carry over' means to transfer something to a later time, not to execute it.
'Carry away' means to remove something physically, not to perform or execute it.
Correct: 'work under a name' means to use that name professionally, often a pseudonym.
'Work with the name' does not have this meaning.
'Work by the name' is not a standard collocation (though 'go by the name' is).
'Work on the name' suggests improving the name itself, not using it as a pseudonym.
Correct: 'the secret lies in doing something' is the fixed pattern for saying what something consists of.
'Lies at choosing' is not a natural collocation.
'Lies on choosing' is not a natural collocation.
'Lies to choosing' is not grammatically possible.
Correct: 'turn down' means to reject a request.
'Put down' means to criticise someone or to euthanise an animal, not to reject a request.
'Let down' means to disappoint someone.
'Knock down' means to demolish something or reduce a price.
Correct: 'however' introduces the contrast with the positive tone of the previous paragraph.
'Moreover' adds a similar point rather than contrasting with it.
'Therefore' signals a result, which does not fit here.
'Besides' adds an extra point rather than introducing a contrast.
Correct: 'take away from something' means to reduce its value or quality.
'Take off from' usually means to depart, which is not the meaning here.
'Take out from' is not a natural collocation with this meaning.
'Take apart' means to disassemble something physically.
Correct: 'there is no doubt that' is the fixed phrase expressing certainty.
'There is no mistake that' is not a natural fixed phrase.
'There is no chance that' means something is very unlikely, the opposite meaning intended.
'There is no worry that' is not a standard fixed phrase.

sets.title: Why We Can't Stop Checking Our Phones
text: Most of us check our phones dozens of times a day, often without even {{1}} aware we are doing it. Psychologists say this habit is largely {{2}} to the way notifications trigger a small reward in the brain.

Each time a message arrives, the brain releases a small amount of dopamine, a chemical associated {{3}} pleasure and motivation. Over time, this can create a cycle that is surprisingly hard to break {{4}} of, even when people know the habit is affecting their sleep or concentration.

Experts suggest a few simple strategies: turning {{5}} notifications for non-essential apps, leaving the phone in another room during meals, and setting specific times to check messages {{6}} than looking constantly. {{7}}, most agree that occasional use is not harmful — the real problem is when checking becomes {{8}}.

why: Correct: 'without even being aware' uses 'being' plus an adjective to describe a state.
'Having aware' is not grammatically possible.
'Getting aware' is not idiomatic; English uses 'become aware' or 'be aware'.
'Doing aware' is not grammatically possible.
Correct: 'is largely due to' is the fixed phrase meaning 'is largely caused by'.
'Result to' is wrong; the correct forms are 'result in' or 'result from'.
'Cause to' needs a different pattern ('cause someone to do something').
'Reason to' needs a different pattern ('a reason to believe something').
Correct: 'associated with' is the standard preposition after 'associated'.
'Associated to' is considered non-standard English.
'Associated on' is not correct.
'Associated for' is not correct.
Correct: 'break free of something' means to escape from a situation that controls you.
'Break clear of' is used for physically escaping an obstacle, not an abstract habit.
'Break loose' is normally followed by 'from', not 'of'.
'Break away' is normally followed by 'from', not 'of'.
Correct: 'turn off' means to deactivate something such as notifications.
'Turn down' means to reduce volume or to reject an offer, not deactivate.
'Turn out' means to result in a particular way or to attend an event.
'Turn over' means to flip something or hand it to someone else.
Correct: 'rather than' means 'instead of' and fits the comparison between two habits.
'Sooner than' relates to time preference, not a choice between two habits here.
'Other than' means 'except for', which reverses the intended meaning.
'Worse than' would mean checking at set times is worse, the opposite of the intended advice.
Correct: 'overall' introduces a summarising conclusion after the list of strategies.
'Moreover' adds a new point rather than summarising.
'Therefore' signals a result from the previous sentence, which does not fit a summary.
'Besides' adds an extra point rather than summarising.
Correct: 'compulsive' describes behaviour driven by an irresistible urge, which is the real problem described.
'Obligatory' means required by a rule, which is not the meaning here.
'Voluntary' means done willingly, which would not describe a problem.
'Occasional' contradicts the sentence, which has just said occasional use is not harmful.
